title: Surface Tension
introduction: A guided introduction to surface forces, interfacial energy, curved surfaces and capillary rise. Build the physical picture, work through the equations and use short checks to test your reasoning.
objectives:
Connect the force and energy descriptions of surface tension.
Count interfaces before selecting an equation.
State the assumptions behind pressure-jump and capillary formulas.
prerequisites:
Basic mechanics and force equilibrium
Work, energy, pressure and density
Elementary geometry and trigonometry

lessons.title: Surface tension: force and energy
lessons.summary: Begin with a soap film, connect force to surface energy and count the interfaces carefully.
lessons.objectives:
Interpret surface tension as force per unit length and energy per unit area.
Explain why a soap film pulls with twice the force of one interface.
Use a force–work argument without confusing projected area with total area.
lessons.prerequisites:
Work done by a constant force
Units and dimensions

body.value:
A liquid interface has an energy cost. Under fixed conditions, a film tends to reduce its area. A movable bar across a soap film is pulled inward by the film.

Surface tension acts tangentially to an interface and perpendicular to the boundary line being considered. The direction matters as much as the magnitude.

components.heading: A film with a movable bar
components.alt: A rectangular soap film pulls a vertical movable bar inward. An external force to the right balances the force of the two film surfaces.
components.caption: Two liquid–air interfaces pull on the bar. L is the wetted length of the bar.
components.description: The film lies in the plane of the page. The bar can slide horizontally along the frame; its weight is not part of this horizontal force balance.

body.value: For a uniform interface, F is the force exerted across a line of length L. The SI unit of surface tension is N m⁻¹.
A thin soap film has two approximately equal liquid–air interfaces. Both pull on the bar, so the total force is F = 2γL when the bar and film geometry match the diagram.

components.heading: Do not add a factor of two automatically

body.value: Count physical interfaces. A liquid drop in air has one interface; a thin soap bubble has two. The fact that an object is drawn with two sides on paper does not determine the count.

Move the bar outward slowly while maintaining the relevant conditions. The total new area includes both film surfaces. The mechanical work increases the interfacial free energy in this idealized description.
N m⁻¹ and J m⁻² are dimensionally identical. For a simple liquid interface under fixed conditions, surface tension links the mechanical and energy descriptions.
A bar of wetted length 5.0 cm is pulled slowly through 2.0 mm against a film with γ = 0.030 N m⁻¹. Find the work done.

hint.value: Use the total area increase of the two interfaces.

solution.value: W = 2γLx = 2 × 0.030 × 0.050 × 0.0020 J. This equals γ times the total area increase, 2Lx.

lessons.title: Curved interfaces and excess pressure
lessons.summary: Distinguish a liquid drop from a soap bubble, then apply the pressure jump with a clear radius convention.
lessons.objectives:
State the pressure jump for a spherical liquid drop.
Distinguish one interface from two in a thin soap bubble.
Use radius consistently in calculations.
lessons.prerequisites:
Surface tension as interfacial energy
Area and volume of a sphere

body.value:
For a spherical liquid drop in a gas, equilibrium requires the internal pressure to exceed the external pressure. Surface tension tends to contract the drop; the pressure difference balances that tendency.

Use R for the radius of the interface. Treat surface tension as uniform, and neglect gravity across the small drop.

components.heading: One interface or two?
components.alt: A liquid drop with one spherical interface has pressure jump two gamma over R. A thin soap bubble with two interfaces has pressure jump approximately four gamma over R.
components.caption: R denotes radius, not diameter. The two soap-bubble radii are treated as equal in the thin-film approximation.
components.description: These formulas compare pressure on opposite sides of the indicated object and assume spherical geometry with uniform surface tension.

body.value: For a small reversible expansion, dA = 8πR dR and dV = 4πR² dR. Equating pressure work to the increase in surface free energy gives the spherical pressure jump.
The inner and outer interfaces each contribute. This expression assumes a film much thinner than R and approximately equal surface tension on both interfaces.
If a problem gives the diameter d, substitute R = d/2. For a liquid drop the pressure jump is 4γ/d, not 2γ/d.
For a spherical drop with R = 2.0 mm and γ = 0.072 N m⁻¹, the excess pressure is 2 × 0.072 / 0.0020 = 72 Pa. This is a pressure difference, not the absolute pressure inside.
The radius of a liquid drop is halved while γ stays constant. What happens to the excess pressure?

hint.value: Look at the inverse dependence on radius.

solution.value: The pressure jump 2γ/R varies inversely with R. This conclusion assumes that the spherical model and constant γ remain valid.

lessons.title: Capillary rise and the contact angle
lessons.summary: Resolve the vertical surface-tension force, define the contact angle through the liquid and see the assumptions behind the familiar formula.
lessons.objectives:
Define the contact angle through the liquid.
Derive the ideal capillary-height relation.
Predict the effects of tube radius and wetting.
lessons.prerequisites:
Vertical force equilibrium
Density and hydrostatic pressure
Trigonometric components of a force

body.value:
The contact angle θ is measured through the liquid between the solid surface and the tangent to the liquid–gas interface at the contact line. For θ less than 90°, cos θ is positive and the ideal model predicts rise. For θ greater than 90°, it predicts depression.

The contact angle depends on the liquid, solid, surrounding medium and surface condition. Do not treat it as a universal property of the liquid alone.

components.heading: Static rise in a narrow tube
components.alt: A wetting liquid rises in a narrow vertical tube above a wide reservoir. The height h is measured from the reservoir free surface; r is the tube radius.
components.caption: The diagram is schematic. The elementary balance neglects the meniscus-volume correction.
components.description: Surface tension around the circular contact line has an upward resultant for a wetting liquid. This balances the effective weight of the raised liquid column in the simplified model.

components.heading: Contact-line force and column weight

body.value: The contact-line length is 2πr. Resolve the surface-tension force vertically and balance it with the weight ρgπr²h. Here r is the internal tube radius, and h is measured relative to the reservoir surface.

components.tex: 2\pi r\gamma\cos\theta=\rho g\pi r^2 h,\qquad h=\frac{2\gamma\cos\theta}{\rho g r}

body.value: Use a uniform vertical narrow tube, static equilibrium, a reservoir much wider than the tube, and approximately constant density and surface tension. The elementary formula neglects the small meniscus volume and treats the outside gas pressure as effectively uniform.

components.heading: There is no generic “capillary suction force”

body.value: Identify the actual interface, contact line and pressure or force balance. Avoid adding an extra upward force after already including surface tension.

components.heading: Water in a clean narrow tube

body.value: For γ = 0.072 N m⁻¹, ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³, g = 9.8 m s⁻², r = 0.50 mm and θ ≈ 0°, the ideal height is about 0.029 m, or 2.9 cm. The numerical estimate depends strongly on the wetting assumption.
What happens to the ideal rise if the tube radius doubles, with the liquid and contact angle unchanged?

solution.value: At fixed γ, ρ, g and θ, h is inversely proportional to r. This predicts equilibrium height, not how quickly the liquid rises.

lessons.title: Extension: where the simple model needs care
lessons.summary: Explore contact-angle hysteresis and nonuniform surface tension without extending the introductory equations beyond their assumptions.
lessons.objectives:
Recognize that advancing and receding contact angles can differ.
Explain why a surface-tension gradient can drive flow.
lessons.prerequisites: Core lessons on surface tension and capillarity

steps.title: A real contact line can stick

body.value:
On real surfaces, roughness and chemical variation can pin a contact line. The advancing contact angle can differ from the receding angle, so a single equilibrium angle may not describe every stage of motion.

When comparing observations with the elementary capillary formula, specify the surface preparation and whether the interface is advancing, receding or stationary.
Two nominally identical tubes show different rise heights. What would you check before concluding that surface tension changed?

answer.value: Check the internal radius, cleanliness, liquid contamination, temperature and wetting or contact-line history.

steps.title: Surface tension need not be uniform

components.heading: A first look at Marangoni flow

body.value:
A surface-tension gradient can produce tangential stress and drive flow along an interface. Temperature or composition differences can create such gradients.

The earlier static formulas assumed uniform γ. Applying them point by point without a complete flow and stress analysis does not describe the resulting motion.

components.heading: A useful boundary for the core model

body.value: First identify the interface geometry, number of interfaces and conditions. Then decide whether static equilibrium, uniform surface tension and a single contact angle are reasonable approximations.
